## Goal

Learn core R syntax and data-handling skills by analyzing the red-spruce fitness-trait dataset you already downloaded in [*Bashing the cluster*](/notebook/posts/bashing-the-cluster/index.qmd), and finish with a first reproducible R script whose outputs land in `results/`.

This module picks up exactly where the cluster exercise left off: `data/raw/` holds the raw file, `src/` will hold your R scripts, and `results/` will hold everything R produces.

#### Prerequisites

- Completed the cluster exercise 
- R (>= 4.2) installed; RStudio recommended but not required
- The dataset available at `data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt`

If you're working locally instead of on the cluster, grab the same file directly from R:

::: {.column-full}
```{r}
#| 
dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anoobvinu07/Genomic_assisted_selection/master/data/FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt",
  destfile = "data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt"
)
```
:::

Recreate the rest of the project layout if you don't already have it:

```{r}

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("src", showWarnings = FALSE)
```


## Learning objectives

By the end of this module you should be able to:

- Start R/RStudio with a reproducible working directory (no hard-coded absolute paths)
- Describe R's core data types and structures: vectors, factors, data frames, lists
- Import and inspect a tab-delimited file
- Subset, filter, and summarize data with base R
- Produce basic plots (histogram, boxplot, scatterplot)
- Save tables and plots into `results/`
- Turn interactive code into a script you can run non-interactively with `Rscript`

#### R quick reference

| Function/operator | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `c()` | Combine values into a vector | `c(1, 2, 3)` |
| `<-` | Assignment | `x <- 5` |
| `read.delim()` | Read a tab-delimited file | `read.delim("data/raw/file.txt")` |
| `str()` | Show structure/types of an object | `str(df)` |
| `dim()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()` | Dimensions of a data frame | `dim(df)` |
| `head()` / `tail()` | First/last rows | `head(df, 5)` |
| `summary()` | Quick numeric/factor summary | `summary(df$Height)` |
| `df$col` | Access a column by name | `df$Fitness` |
| `df[rows, cols]` | Subset by position/condition | `df[df$Region == "E", ]` |
| `table()` | Count occurrences | `table(df$Population)` |
| `tapply()` / `aggregate()` | Grouped summaries | `tapply(df$Height, df$Population, mean)` |
| `function(...) {}` | Define a function | `f <- function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `for (i in seq)` | Loop | `for (p in unique(df$Population)) {...}` |
| `hist()`, `boxplot()`, `plot()` | Base R plotting | `hist(df$Height)` |
| `write.csv()` | Save a table | `write.csv(x, "results/out.csv")` |

## Setting up your R project

On the cluster, load R and start it from inside `cluster-exercise/`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false

cd ~/projects/cluster-exercise

module biocontainers/default
module load r          # module name may differ on your cluster; check `module avail r`

R                      # start the R session
```


Inside R, always confirm where you are before reading or writing anything:

```{r}
getwd()
```

If you're using RStudio, create an RStudio Project (`File > New Project`) rooted at `cluster-exercise/` — this keeps every path relative and portable, exactly like the `data/raw/...` paths from the bash module.

## R data types and structures

```{r}
# Vectors: one-dimensional, single type
heights <- c(27.3, 31.1, 29.6, 32.0)
pops    <- c("AB", "AB", "CC", "CC")

# Factors: categorical vectors with fixed levels
region <- factor(c("E", "E", "C", "C"))
levels(region)

# Data frames: a table — columns can be different types
df_demo <- data.frame(pop = pops, height = heights)
str(df_demo)

# Lists: can hold mixed, differently-shaped objects
result <- list(mean_height = mean(heights), populations = unique(pops))
result$mean_height
```

**Key idea:** almost everything you do in this module is a data frame — one row per tree, one column per variable — with vectors as its columns.

### Importing and inspecting the dataset

```{r}
traits <- read.delim("data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt",
                      header = TRUE, sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dim(traits)          # rows x columns
names(traits)        # column names
str(traits)          # types per column
head(traits, 5)      # first 5 rows
summary(traits$Height)
```

You should see 19 columns including identifiers (`Family`, `Population`, `Tree`, `Location`, `Region`), coordinates and environment (`Latitude`, `Longitude`, `Elevation`), fitness traits (`SeedWeight`, `Germination`, `Survival`, `Height`, `Fitness`), and genetic parameters (`PC1`, `PC2`, `Family_Homozygosity`, `Population_Homozygosity`, `Genetic_Diversity`, `Genetic_Load`) — we'll use that last group in Module 2.

**Don't assume a column's type from its name** — Always check with `str()` before analyzing.

### Indexing and subsetting

```{r}
# A single column
traits$Fitness |> head() # |> head() : pipe (|>) the additional commands (head()) at the end 

# Rows meeting a condition
edge <- traits[traits$Region == "E", ]
nrow(edge)

# Multiple conditions
healthy_edge <- traits[traits$Region == "E" & traits$Survival > 0.8, ]

# subset() reads more like a sentence
subset(traits, Region == "E" & Height > 35, select = c(Population, Height, Fitness))
```

### Summarizing data

```{r}
# Counts
table(traits$Population) # number of inds per population
table(traits$Region)     # number of inds per region

# Grouped means with tapply()
tapply(traits$Height, traits$Population, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

# Grouped summary with aggregate()
aggregate(cbind(Height, Fitness) ~ Population, data = traits, FUN = mean) |> head()
```

### Basic plotting

:::{.panel-tabset}
#### Default Histogram
```{r}
hist(traits$SeedWeight, main = "Seed weight distribution", 
        xlab = "Seed weight")
```

#### Breaks = 30
```{r}
hist(traits$SeedWeight, main = "Seed weight distribution", 
        xlab = "Seed weight", breaks = 30)
```


#### Breaks = 50
```{r}
hist(traits$SeedWeight, main = "Seed weight distribution", 
        xlab = "Seed weight", breaks = 50)
```
:::

```{r}
boxplot(Height ~ Region, data = traits, 
        main = "Height by region", 
        ylab = "Height (cm)")
```

```{r}
plot(traits$Elevation, traits$Fitness,
     xlab = "Elevation (m)", ylab = "Fitness",
     main = "Fitness vs elevation")
```

### Saving outputs and scripting

```{r}
pop_summary <- aggregate(cbind(Height, Fitness, SeedWeight) ~ Population, data = traits, FUN = mean)
write.csv(pop_summary, "results/population_trait_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

# exporting plot as a .png
png("results/height_by_region.png", width = 800, height = 600)
boxplot(Height ~ Region, data = traits)
dev.off()
```

Put everything into `src/01_explore_traits.R` and run it non-interactively — this is what makes it reproducible and Slurm-friendly:

```{bash}
#| eval: false

Rscript src/01_explore_traits.R
```

## Wrap up  
### Idea check

Answer these in your own words before moving to the exercises — write your answers as comments at the top of `src/01_explore_traits.R`.

1. What is the difference between a vector and a data frame in R?
2. Why prefer a relative path like `"data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt"` over an absolute path like `/home/your_username/...`?
3. What does `str(traits)` tell you that `head(traits)` does not?
4. Why does treating `Region` as a `factor` (rather than plain character text) matter for `boxplot(Height ~ Region, data = traits)`?
5. If `mean(traits$Height)` returned `NA`, what would you check first, and how would you fix it?
6. Why write outputs into `results/` instead of overwriting anything in `data/raw/`?

### Practical exercises

Work through these in order inside an R session, then consolidate the working code into `src/01_explore_traits.R`.

1. Load the dataset and confirm it has 326 rows and 19 columns.
2. Run `str(traits)` and list every column name along with its type (`chr`, `int`, `num`).
3. Compute overall summary statistics (mean, sd, min, max) for `Height` and `Fitness`.
4. Use `table()` to count trees per `Population` and per `Region`. Which population has the most trees sampled?
5. Subset the data to trees in `Region == "C"` with `Survival > 0.8`. How many trees meet this criterion?
6. Use `aggregate()` or `tapply()` to get mean `Height` and mean `Fitness` per `Population`. Identify the top 3 populations by mean `Fitness`.
7. Create a histogram of `SeedWeight` and a boxplot of `Height` by `Region`. Save both as PNG files in `results/`.
8. Save your population-level summary table as `results/population_trait_summary.csv`.
9. Move all working code into `src/01_explore_traits.R` and confirm it runs cleanly end-to-end with `Rscript src/01_explore_traits.R`, producing the expected files in `results/`.

### Homework 

- Compute summary statistics (mean, sd, min, max) for at least **4 traits** (e.g., `Height`, `Fitness`, `SeedWeight`, `Germination`), broken down by both `Population` and `Region`.
- Produce at least **3 plots**: one histogram, one boxplot grouped by `Region`, and one scatterplot relating two continuous variables (e.g., `Elevation` vs. `Fitness`). Save all three to `results/`.
- Write your interpretation as comments at the bottom of the script, answering:
  - Which population has the highest and lowest mean fitness?
  - Is there a visible relationship between elevation and fitness or seed weight? Describe it in one or two sentences.
- **Bonus (optional):** recreate one plot with `ggplot2` instead of base R.
